summary: Presents an experimental architecture for an agent system that offers sophisticated ways to access and manage information on the Internet. It is a research proposal, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine helpful robot assistants that fetch and organize things from the internet for you. This note sketches how such helpers might work.

questions: how do uras encapsulate internet activities
subtitle: Agent architecture for encapsulating Internet information access activities

tldr.problem: Internet resources and services are heterogeneous, and accessing them requires protocol-specific knowledge that must be embedded in every application; there is no standard way to specify a high-level information access activity that can be reused or transported.
tldr.mechanism: Uniform Resource Agents (URAs) are persistent, portable software objects that encapsulate the steps needed to carry out an Internet activity, including the target resources, required data, the activity workflow, and response filtering. A URAgency runtime executes URAs and handles different URA types.
tldr.outcome: Applications can delegate information access tasks to URAs, which isolate them from protocol details while allowing activities to be specified once and reused or modified by others. The architecture was experimental; later agent and service technologies pursued different approaches.

facts.label: URA components
facts.value: 6 (Header, Activation Data, Targets, Experience, Activity, Response Filter)

today: RFC 2016 is an Experimental Protocol. URAs as described here did not become a standard mechanism. The broader landscape of Internet agents, web services, APIs, and automation frameworks evolved differently—toward REST APIs, web services, JavaScript in browsers, and modern agent architectures. However, the core idea of encapsulating complex workflows and making them portable and reusable has remained influential in service-oriented architectures and workflow automation tools.

sections.title: Problem and Motivation
sections.content:
The World Wide Web has made diverse Internet resources accessible, but the predominant activity is human browsing—looking at one document at a time. For higher-level activities such as searching multiple web resources and news groups on a topic, or subscribing to mailing lists across different servers, every application must contain protocol-aware code. This limits applications to the types of services foreseen by their creators.

The RFC proposes that Internet information access should be abstracted at a higher level. The goal is to specify an activity with the same precision and reusability accorded to resource naming (via URLs) and identification. Uniform Resource Agents are designed to encapsulate knowledge about relevant Internet resources and the mechanisms required to access them, allowing invokers (whether human or other software) to delegate entire sets of tasks without understanding the underlying protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now, every program that wants to search the internet has to be taught how to search. It would be better if one helper could do the searching and any program could ask that helper to find things.

sections.title: URA Architecture and Components
sections.content:
A URA is a persistent software object that captures a complete Internet activity. The specification centres on the URAgency, which is a runtime environment that understands how to execute URAs. A URAgency identifies the types of URAs it supports and applies methods to instantiate and execute them.

The RFC defines six core components of a URA object: a URA Header (identifying the agent, its type, creator and dependencies); Activation Data (the input fields or parameters the invoker must provide); Targets (the URLs or URNs of Internet resources to access); Experience Information (data stored between invocations); Activity (a script specifying which targets to contact and under what conditions); and a Response Filter (a script that transforms raw responses into the final result). Each component is specified in a standardized virtual structure, allowing URAs to be portable across different URAgencies and implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: A URA is like a recipe card: it says what ingredients you need, which stores to visit, what order to visit them in, and how to combine what you get into a final answer.

sections.title: Execution and Composition
sections.content:
To use a URA, an invoker provides values for the Activation Data fields (such as search keywords or email address) or identifies a saved URA instance. The URAgency then executes the Activity script, which instantiates the target URLs and contacts each service in sequence, applying conditional logic based on which data fields were provided or whether previous services succeeded. The Response Filter script then processes the raw responses from all contacted services and formats them into the final result.

Because URAs have a standardized structure, they can act as invokers of other URAs. This enables composition: a top-level URA can orchestrate multiple specialized URAs, each responsible for one type of service or data source. For example, a book-shopping URA might delegate to specialized URAs for each online bookstore, maintaining a clear separation of concerns. URAs can also be chained, with one URA outputting data suitable as input to another.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask the helper to search for books, it might ask three different bookstores, collect all their answers, sort them, and give you the results ranked by price.

sections.title: Example Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC motivates URAs with practical scenarios. A mailing list subscription URA encapsulates the steps needed to subscribe a user to different types of mail servers, each with different protocols and subscription procedures. Instead of embedding subscription code in every email client, all applications delegate to the subscription URA, which handles the variation.

A software search URA illustrates composition: it searches multiple sources (Archie servers, FTP sites, web indexes) relevant to the topic. The URA creator can also use variables for resources that change by location—for example, a Canadian Archie server for Canadian users and a different one for Australian users—so the same URA works in different contexts without modification. A news search URA (shown in a prototype example) searches Usenet news via the DejaNews service and reformats results into a standardized output format.
sections.plainLanguage: One URA knows how to subscribe to mailing lists everywhere. Another knows how to find software. If you need both, you just ask both helpers, and they work together.

sections.title: Prototype Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC describes a prototype implementation using the Tcl scripting language for URA definitions. The URAgency was integrated into the Silk Desktop Internet Resource Discovery tool, a graphical interface that presents a list of available URAs to the user. For each activity, Silk prompts the user for Activation Data and executes the URA. Users can create new URAs by writing Tcl scripts following the URA Writer's Guide, and Silk manages URA instances.

The prototype demonstrated the feasibility of the approach and identified challenges: services are often designed for human users and output HTML or plain text formats that are fragile to parse. When a service changes its output format, a URA that depends on exact field positions breaks. The RFC notes that service providers could distribute URAs that they maintain themselves, ensuring that URAs stay in sync with service interface changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The team built a program called Silk that lets you pick from a list of helpers and tells them what you want. The helpers are written in a simple computer language, and experts can create new ones.

sections.title: Status and Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 2016 is an Experimental Protocol. It was an early research proposal in the evolution of Internet information services and user agents. While the work was still in experimental stages, it inspired interest in more sophisticated mechanisms for accessing diverse Internet resources.

The RFC acknowledges that other approaches to Internet agents (such as Java applets, mobile code systems, and domain-specific agent architectures) pursue different trade-offs. URAs differ by focusing on high-level activities and information services rather than generic mobile objects. The core challenge of service interface brittleness (formats changing, breaking parsers) remains an ongoing problem in any agent-based information access system. The RFC suggests that standardized 'service entrances' offering structured data instead of human-readable output could reduce this fragility.
sections.plainLanguage: This was an experimental idea that showed promise but faced challenges. Since the Internet has evolved a lot, people now use different kinds of helpers and tools.
